question: What did you say in your first address at the Parliament of Religions in Chicago?

result.text: As I told the audience at the Parliament of Religions in Chicago, it fills my heart with joy unspeakable to rise in response to the warm and cordial welcome which you have given us.[1] I thanked them in the name of the most ancient order of monks in the world; I thanked them in the name of the mother of religions; and I thanked them in the name of millions and millions of Hindu people of all classes and sects.[1] I expressed my gratitude for the opportunity to represent Hinduism at the Parliament of Religions, which I believed would be ably upheld by its representative in that memorable religious assembly.[2] I emphasized that the doctrines of Hinduism, when clearly and authoritatively presented, would produce a remarkable impression and inspire many to seek the spiritual truths of Indian philosophy.[2] I called attention to the characteristic Hindu doctrine of the Harmony and Brotherhood of Religions, which I believed would lead to a larger, fuller, and holier evolution of humanity.[2] I stated that no longer could it be insisted that Truth and Holiness were the exclusive possessions of any particular locality or system of doctrine.[2] I quoted from the Bhagavad-Gitâ, saying that the whole world of religions is only a travelling, a coming up of different men and women through various conditions and circumstances to the same goal.[2]

question: How did your view of Buddhism relate to Hinduism in your Chicago addresses?

result.text: I explained that Buddhism is not a separate religion but a development of Hinduism, much like how Christianity is a development of Judaism.[1] I emphasized that Shâkya Muni, the Buddha, was a Hindu who came to fulfill the teachings of Hinduism, not to destroy them.[1] I stated that the difference between modern Buddhism and the teachings of Lord Buddha lies in the misunderstanding by his followers, not in the teachings themselves.[1] I argued that the Buddha was not a new teacher but a fulfillment of the old Hindu religion, just as Jesus was a fulfillment of the Old Testament.[1] I made it clear that I do not criticize the Buddha, whom I worship as God incarnate on earth, but rather the misinterpretation of his teachings by his followers.[1]

question: What did you write to Alasinga about starting work in Madras?

result.text: I wrote to Alasinga from the U. S. a on 1894-08-31 that I had Rs. 9,000 with me, part of which I would send to him for the organisation, and I would get many people to send money to him in Madras yearly, half-yearly, or monthly.[1] I told Alasinga that he should start a Society and a journal and the necessary apparatus, and that this must be a secret amongst only a few.[1] I advised Alasinga to collect funds from Mysore and elsewhere to build a temple in Madras which should have a library and some rooms for the office and the preachers who should be Sannyâsins, and for Vairâgis who may chance to come.[1] I wrote to Alasinga from New York on 1894-04-09 that the resolution would be of such a nature that the Hindu community of Madras, who sent me over, expressing its entire satisfaction in my work here.[2] I told Alasinga that I had done a good deal of work this year and hoped to do a good deal more in the next, and that he should not bother about the missionaries.[3] I wrote to Alasinga from the U. S. a on 1894-08-31 that I had seen an editorial on me about the circular from Madras in the Boston Transcript, and that nothing had reached me yet.[4]

question: What did you say about the condition of the masses in India?

result.text: I remarked that the masses in India are very good because poverty here is not a crime.[1] I noted that our masses are not violent, unlike what I often experienced in America and England.[1] I described the masses as being much more civilised than the European masses in every other respect.[1] I explained that the masses, through ages of constant tyranny of the higher castes, have totally lost their manliness and become like professional beggars.[2] I pointed out that the highly-educated, prominent men among the masses form societies and clamour for more from the English rulers.[2] I stated that the great national sin is the neglect of the masses, and that no amount of politics would be of any avail until they are well educated, well fed, and well cared for.[3] I argued that caste is a very good thing and that the plan in India is to make everybody a Brahmin, the Brahmin being the ideal of humanity.[4]

question: What was your position on the caste system?

result.text: I argued that the caste system was a hereditary trade guild, not a religious institution, and that it had been in existence from time immemorial.[1] I stated that the caste system was opposed to the religion of the Vedanta, and that all our great preachers have tried to break it down.[2] I explained that the caste system had a great side, as it rejected competition, but it also checked individuality.[3] I said that the caste system was a social custom, and that it was simply the outgrowth of the political institutions of India.[2] I mentioned that the caste system had very good things in it, but for myself, I would not have any caste if Lord helps me.[3] I noted that the caste system was a rigid, high power that had made the nation live while other nations have died, but it also had a great evil: it checked individuality.[3] I said that the caste system was not a granted [graded] system of classes, but that each caste thought itself to be superior to all the others.[1]

question: What did you say about the education of women in India?

result.text: I argued that women in India have the potential to become ideal women in the world if given the right sort of education.[1] I pointed out that in the West, women often seem to be replicas of men, whereas in India, feminine modesty and reserve are a source of comfort.[1] I noted that only three or four per cent of the people in India are educated, and not even one per cent of the women.[2] I mentioned that Calcutta University opened its doors to women more than twenty years ago, and girls graduated with the same standard as boys.[3] I emphasized that our religion does not prevent a woman from being educated, and that women should be trained in this way.[3] I stated that our right of interference is limited entirely to giving education, and that women must be put in a position to solve their own problems in their own way.[4] I said that Indian women are as capable of solving their own problems as any in the world.[4]

question: How did you describe your Master, Shri Ramakrishna, in your lectures?

result.text: I described my Master, Shri Ramakrishna, as a living illustration of the ideas he preached, which made his life particularly interesting.[1] I emphasized that his mind was continually conscious of God, dedicated to Him utterly, and would not be used for any other purpose.[2] I noted that he refused to think of body and illness, instead focusing his mental power on the divine.[2] I mentioned that his teachings revealed a wonderful unity underlying everything, discovered in Hinduism, Islam, and Christianity.[3] I highlighted that his legacy inspired a lifelong struggle to live the life he taught, not just to talk about it.[4] I pointed out that his influence grew significantly over time, with celebrations of his birthday increasing from a hundred to fifty thousand people.[4] I expressed that his teachings and example continue to be revered and spread widely across India.[4]

question: What did you tell the people of Madras when you returned from the West?

result.text: As I returned to India after my visit to the West, several orthodox Hindus raised a howl against my association with the Western people and my breaking the rules of orthodoxy.[1] They did not like me to teach the truths of the Vedas to the people of the West.[1] On behalf of your Hindu co-religionists in Madras, we offer you a most hearty welcome on the occasion of your return from your Religious Mission in the West.[2] Our object in approaching you with this address is not the performance of any merely formal or ceremonial function; we come to offer you the love of our hearts and to give expression to our feeling of thankfulness for the services which you, by the grace of God, have been able to render to the great cause of Truth by proclaiming India's lofty religious ideals.[2] I wish to take this early opportunity of your arrival and reception at Madras to express my feelings of joy and pleasure on your safe return to India and to offer my heartfelt congratulation on the great success which has attended your unselfish efforts in Western lands.[3] Your labours have now proved beyond the possibility of doubt that the contradictions of the world's numerous creeds are all reconciled in the universal light of the Vedanta.[3] And I in common with my people pray that the blessings of God may rest on you and your labours.[3]

question: What did you say about idol worship when questioned in the West?

result.text: I was asked in the West what my attitude was towards Western religions, and I spoke about the differences in religious practices between Hindus and Christians.[1] I explained that a man may be learned in the Western sense but may not know the basics of religion, and I questioned whether he could think of spirit as such or had manifested his soul above matter.[2] I noted that for the poor, idols were necessary for worship, and that in ancient times, women were distinguished for spiritual genius and strength of mind.[3] I addressed the criticism that I had previously criticized the Tantras but now supported the worship of women as taught in them, and I clarified that I was not contradicting myself.[4] I asked the monk what he worshipped and what his idea of God was, emphasizing the importance of understanding the nature of the divine.[5] I stated that we Hindus do not reject any new idea but try to harmonize it, as taught by Shri Krishna, who proclaimed himself as the inspirer of all religions.[6] I mentioned that I had been asked by Christians what they thought of when they prayed, and some said they thought of the church, others of God.[3]

question: What did you write about the relationship between science and religion?

result.text: I wrote that the fight between science and religion arises because religions are encumbered with explanations from outside, such as angels in charge of natural elements.[1] I explained that science seeks the cause of a thing by examining its nature itself, unlike religion, which often attributes causes to external spirits.[1] I argued that Advaitism is the most scientific religion because it explains spiritual matters without relying on external causes, just as science explains natural phenomena.[1] I stated that religion, like science, deals with truths of the metaphysical world, and the book from which to learn religion is one's own mind and heart.[2] I noted that the mind is in a constant state of flux, and our ideas concerning religion are changing all the time, which makes it seem less certain than other sciences.[3] I compared the search for unity in religion to the search for elements in chemistry, suggesting that both sciences aim to reach a perfect unity and thus become complete.[4][5] I emphasized that religion belongs to the supersensuous and not to the sense plane, being beyond reasoning and intellect, and a plunge into the unknown and unknowable.[6]

question: What did you say about Christ in your lecture 'Christ, the Messenger'?

result.text: I spoke about the great lesson of the Messenger, which is renunciation, and how it is the basis of all religions.[1] I explained that renunciation is about unselfishness and that the ideal is perfect unselfishness, such as turning the other cheek when struck.[1] I mentioned that Jesus told a rich young man to sell all his possessions and give to the poor, and that this is the one ideal he preaches.[1] I emphasized that the voice of renunciation rings in our ears even in the midst of worldly things, urging us to give up all that we have and follow Christ.[1] I described Jesus as a disembodied, unfettered, unbound spirit who saw all men and women as embodiments of the same undying spirit.[2] I stated that Jesus called upon people to realize their own spiritual nature and to think that they are not slaves but immortal spirits.[2] I quoted Jesus saying, 'Know, the Kingdom of Heaven is within you,' and urged people to feel that they are one with God.[2]

question: What did you say about Mohammedanism and Islam?

result.text: As I spoke at the lecture on The Way to the Realisation of a Universal Religion, I emphasized that all old religions, including Mohammedanism, have kept their great mission intact despite their mistakes and difficulties.[1] I noted that Mohammedanism, despite being hated by some Christian people, promotes practical brotherhood among all its followers, regardless of race, caste, creed, or sex.[1][2] I pointed out that in Mohammedanism, there is no distinction made between people, and even a Negro or an American Indian who becomes a Mohammedan is treated as a brother by the Sultan of Turkey.[1][2] I remarked that in many places in the Koran, there are very sensual ideas of life, but what Mohammedanism truly comes to preach is the practical brotherhood of all its followers.[1] I stated that there is not one word in the Koran which says that women have no souls, and that it actually affirms that women have souls.[3] I expressed that the Vedantic spirit of religious liberality has very much affected Mohammedanism in India, making it quite different from that in other countries.[4] I said that I love our Mohammedans, showing a deep respect and affection for them.[5]

question: What were your views on the Vedas and their authority?

result.text: I argued that the Vedas are not the utterance of any person, but rather the eternal knowledge of God, existing throughout time without beginning or end.[1] I stated that the Vedas were not written or created by any individual, but were discovered by Rishis, who were seers of thought that already existed in the universe.[1] I emphasized that the Vedas are the primary authority in Hinduism, and that all other religious texts, such as the Puranas and Tantras, are subordinate to them.[2] I explained that the Vedas were never written, and that their ideas evolved slowly until they were embodied in book form, becoming the authority for Hindu thought.[3] I noted that the Vedas are not historical in nature, unlike other scriptures, and that their non-historicity is in their favor, as they are not man-made.[2] I stated that only those portions of the Vedas which agree with reason should be accepted as authority, while other Shâstras, such as the Purânas, are to be accepted only so far as they do not go against the Vedas.[4] I pointed out that the Vedas are the foundation of all religious thought in the world, and that all subsequent religious ideas have been derived from them.[4]

question: How did you explain Maya in your London lectures?

result.text: I explained that Maya is not a theory, but a statement of facts about the universe as it exists.[1] I emphasized that Maya is the combination of the three ideas Desha-Kâla-Nimitta — space, time, and causation — and this time and space and cause have been further reduced into Nâma-Rupa.[2] I used the example of a wave in the ocean to illustrate that the wave is distinct from the ocean only in its form and name, and this form and this name cannot have any separate existence from the wave.[2] I stated that Maya is what makes the difference between me and you, between all animals and man, between gods and men.[2] I explained that Maya is the energy of the universe, potential and kinetic, and that until Mother releases us, we cannot get free.[3] I mentioned that the theory of Maya was manipulated a little by the Buddhists too, but in the hands of the Buddhists it became very much like what is called Idealism.[4] It is a simple statement of facts — what we are and what we see around us.[4]

question: What did you say about the Sikhs and Guru Govind Singh?

result.text: I spoke of Guru Govind Singh during a conversation at Balaram Babu's residence at Baghbazar, where I recounted his life and the revival of the Sikh sect through his renunciation and austerities.[1] I mentioned that Guru Govind Singh united both Hindus and Muslims within the fold of his religion, leading them towards the same end, an example rare in Indian history.[2] I explained that Guru Govind Singh did not create a common interest but pointed out the injustice and oppression of his time, which drew both Hindus and Muslims to him.[3] I described Guru Govind Singh as a great worshipper of Shakti, and noted that his example of unity and spiritual strength is indeed very rare in Indian history.[3] I quoted a popular Sikh Dohâ that illustrates the power infused into initiates by Guru Govind Singh, emphasizing his ability to inspire strength in his followers.[1] I emphasized that Guru Govind Singh's example of love and forgiveness, even when betrayed, is a model for all to follow, and that such a man is worthy of the name Hindu.[4] I noted that Guru Govind Singh's spiritual work led to the political organization of the Sikhs, following a spiritual upheaval that eventually strengthened the spiritual aspirations of the people.[5]

question: What did you write to Sister Nivedita about her work for Indian women?

result.text: I wrote to Sister Nivedita from Darjeeling on April 3, 1897, informing her of a bit of important work for her to do on behalf of the downtrodden masses of India.[1] In a letter dated April 4, 1901, I told Sister Nivedita that she should stay as long as she thought she was working well.[2] I also mentioned that Yum had some talk about her with Mother, and that Mother desired her to come over, though it was only out of love and anxiety to see her.[2] In another letter, I expressed my hope that Sister Nivedita would continue her work for India by her pen, as I joined in earnest prayer with the hopes of her future services to India.[3] I also wrote to Sister Nivedita from Gopal Lal Villa on March 4, 1902, asking her to open letters directed to me if I passed away and to send the girl back home if she had no money to go back.[4]

question: What did you say about vegetarianism and meat-eating?

result.text: I wrote that vegetarianism had its beginning in India, and that the fear of eating one's ancestors could not affect those who propagate it.[1] I argued that taking the life of a few goats as against the inability to protect the honour of one's own wife and daughter, and to save the morsels for one's children from robbing hands — which of these is more sinful?[2] I stated that the taking of life is undoubtedly sinful; but so long as vegetable food is not made suitable to the human system through progress in chemistry, there is no other alternative but meat-eating.[2] I taught meat-eating throughout the length and breadth of India in the hope that we can build a militant spirit.[3] I said that for him surely is a strict vegetarian diet whose one end is to lead solely a spiritual life.[4] I wrote that the nations who take the animal food are always, as a rule, notably brave, heroic and thoughtful.[5] I said that the very sight of meat will disgust you, and there will come a time when you cannot possibly eat it.[6]

question: What was your opinion of social reformers in India?

result.text: I wrote in my essay on the Social Conference Address that there are problems in Indian society that neither I nor my Western Guru can yet grasp the meaning of — much less solve.[1] I asked in my essay on the Social Conference Address, what support, what pay, do the mendicants receive in India, compared to the pay and privilege of our social reformers?[2] In my lecture on the Mission of the Vedanta, I stated that I am neither a caste-breaker nor a mere social reformer, and that I have nothing to do directly with your castes or with your social reformation.[3] I told the audience at Colombo that for nearly the past one hundred years, our country has been flooded with social reformers and various social reform proposals, but that this one hundred years of social reform has produced no permanent and valuable result appreciable throughout the country.[3] In my interview, I said that the reason for the lack of results from social reform movements is that they have been inconsiderate imitations of Western means and methods of work, which will not do for India.[4] I told the audience at Colombo that the difference between ancient reformers and modern reformers is that the ancient ones had not the fanfaronade of the reformers of today; they had no curses on their lips as modern reformers have; their lips pronounced only blessings.[5] Vain is it to attempt the lines of action that foreign societies have engrafted upon us; it is impossible.[5]

question: What did you say about the Theosophists?

result.text: I wrote to my brave boys that the Theosophical magazines saying they prepared the way to my success is pure nonsense.[1] In my lecture on my plan of campaign, I acknowledged that the Theosophical Society has done some good work for India, and I expressed gratitude to Mrs. Besant for her efforts.[2] I told the audience that the Theosophists did not help me in my achievements in America and England, and that every word of such claims is wrong and untrue.[2] In a letter to Alasinga, I warned that any suspicion of my connection with the Theosophists would spoil my work in America and England, and that they are thought by people of sound mind to be wrong.[3] I mentioned that in India, Theosophists and Buddhists are nonentities, only publishing a few papers and trying to catch Occidental ears.[4] I stated that I do not care a fig for what the missionaries or the Theosophists say about me, and that taking notice of them gives them importance.[5] I told Swami Brahmananda that the Theosophists and others wanted to intimidate me, and that I had to give them a bit of my mind to clear my position.[6]

question: What did you say about the English and British rule in India?

result.text: I wrote to Miss Mary Hale from Ridgely Manor on 1899-10-30 that British rule in modern India has only one redeeming feature, though unconscious; it has brought India out once more on the stage of the world; it has forced upon it the contact of the outside world.[1] In an interview, I said that but for the English rule I could not be here, and that it is through the intermixture of English blood and ideas that the salvation of India will come.[2] I told a monk that but for English rule I could not be here now, though your lowest free-born American Negro holds higher position in India politically than is mine.[3] I wrote that the English public is forming the idea that the passing away of the Indian Empire from their sway will end in imminent peril to the English nation, and be their ruin.[4] I noted that the Hindu sects of the century seem to have set one ideal of truth before them — the approval of their English masters.[5] I stated that the Indian nation is by far the most moral and religious nation in the whole world, and it would be a blasphemy to compare the Hindus with any other nation.[6]

question: What did you tell Mrs. Bull about your plans for the Math at Belur?

result.text: I wrote to Mrs. Bull that I had given her a chance to draw her money out of the Math, and as she did not say anything about it, I got the trust deeds executed at the British Consulate.[1] I told Mrs. Bull that I was in Benaras for a few days and that all letters should be addressed to the Belur Math.[2] I informed Mrs. Bull that I was in Calcutta for rest and quiet and that I was there because it was best for my health.[3] I mentioned to Mrs. Bull that I had made a discovery about the mental method of practising what the Gita teaches, of working without an eye to results.[4] I wrote to Mrs. Bull that I was in the vale of death and that I had been suffering from a disease that gave me the sensation of suffocation.[3] I told Mrs. Bull that I was in Calcutta for rest and quiet and that I was there because it was best for my health.[3]

question: What did you write about the historical evolution of India?

result.text: I wrote that non-existence can never be the cause of what exists, and that something cannot come out of nothing.[1] I stated that the law of causation is omnipotent and has existed since the time of the Aryan race, as sung by ancient poet-seers and formulated by philosophers.[1] I emphasized that this law is the cornerstone upon which the Hindu man of today builds his whole scheme of life.[1] I wrote that the historical evolution of India is rooted in the ancient history, which is full of descriptions of the gigantic energies and their multifarious workings, the boundless spirit, and the profound thoughtfulness of a godly race.[2] I noted that although the heaps of triumphal flags gathered in India's victories over nature have been torn and tattered by adverse circumstances, they still proclaim the glory of Ancient India.[2] I wrote that the ancient history of India does not possess a history in the narrow sense of narratives of kings and emperors, but rather reveals the exact position and every step made in advance by the vast body of men who impelled by hunger and thirst, lust and greed, etc., arrived through various ways and means at that stage of eminence.[2]

question: What did you say to your brother disciples about organising the Ramakrishna Mission?

result.text: I wrote to my brother disciples at Alambazar Monastery that the Society was named the Ramakrishna Mission after the future programme was discussed.[1] I told my brother disciples that we must mix with all and alienate none, and that we should not insist upon everybody's believing in our Guru.[2] I instructed my brother disciples to start a permanent preaching centre wherever they went, and to edit a magazine that would be half Bengali and half Hindi, and if possible, another in English.[2] I urged my brother disciples to open the eyes of the poor and ignorant by going to their cottages and giving them oral teaching, and to slowly extend their centres.[3] I expressed my fear that the worship-room might become an obsession with old-fashioned ceremonials, and that people might waste their energy in ringing bells instead of doing real work.[4] I told my brother disciples that I was ready to lay down my life to help spread Shri Ramakrishna's teachings all over the world, regardless of whether people accepted his name or not.[4] I wrote to my brother disciples that I had heard everything about Brother Tarak from Madras and that they were highly pleased with him, and that if he went to Madras, a lot of work would be done there.[5]

question: What did you say about Shankaracharya and Advaita?

result.text: I wrote in my book that Shankaracharya was one of the last representatives of the Advaita system, which existed ages before he was born.[1] I pointed out that Shankaracharya made mistakes by supposing that the whole of the Upanishads taught one thing, which was Advaitism, and nothing else.[2] I noted that Shankaracharya and his disciples have been the great preachers of Advaita both in Southern and in Northern India.[3] I stated that Shankaracharya revivified the Vedanta philosophy and made it a rationalistic philosophy.[4] I mentioned that Shankaracharya's movement has entirely swallowed up and assimilated several non-dualistic sects.[3] I remarked that Shankaracharya's Advaita philosophy is not the only one that can be called Vedanta, as all three systems — Advaita, Vishishtadvaita, and dualism — are covered by the word Vedanta.[1] I noted that Shankaracharya's Advaita philosophy is not the only one that can be called Vedanta, as all three systems — Advaita, Vishishtadvaita, and dualism — are covered by the word Vedanta.[1]

question: What did you say about Ramanuja and qualified non-dualism?

result.text: I explained that Ramanuja held the view that the soul is Anu, like a particle, very small, while the followers of Shankaracharya hold that it is Vibhu, omnipresent.[1] I noted that the qualified non-dualists express the soul's purity and perfection becoming contracted and again manifest, and that we are trying to remanifest the intelligence, purity, and power natural to the soul.[2] I stated that the qualified non-dualists believe the soul is a part of God, and that each soul has the same goal of living with God forever.[2] I mentioned that the qualified non-dualists see God as a Personal God, the repository of infinite blessed qualities, interpenetrating everything in the universe.[2] I emphasized that the qualified non-dualists do not deny the soul's individuality, but rather see it as a part of the infinite God.[2]

question: What did you say about the Buddha as a person?

result.text: I spoke of the Buddha as a man who was bereft of all motive power, giving up his throne and everything else to preach for the good of men and animals with a heart as wide as the ocean.[1] I expressed deep veneration for the character of the Buddha, noting his boldness, fearlessness, and tremendous love for the good of all.[2] I described the Buddha as a man who did not seek truth for himself, but sought it because people were in misery, and his only concern was how to help them.[2] I emphasized that the Buddha was born for the good of the many, as a blessing to the many, and that he did not go to the forest to meditate for his own salvation, but to find a way out of the world's suffering.[3] I recounted how the Buddha, when faced with five young men quarreling over the nature of God, asked them if they had ever seen God, and they all answered no, leading him to question their own ignorance and suggest they be pure and good.[4] I stated that the Buddha was one of whom his friends or enemies could never say that he drew a breath or ate a crumb of bread but for the good of all.[5] I noted that the Buddha was a great preacher of the brotherhood of mankind, teaching that all people, regardless of race or caste, have the same right to God and to religion and to freedom.[4] I mentioned that the Buddha was a great man who stood head and shoulders above all other men, and that his followers could never say he did anything but for the good of all.[5]

question: What did you say about the role of the Brahmin in India's future?

result.text: As I spoke at Colombo, I emphasized that the Brahmin must work hard to raise the Indian people by teaching them what they know and giving out the culture they have accumulated for centuries.[1] I argued that the Brahmin's duty is to open the treasury of virtue and distribute its valuables to the world, as Manu says, because with him is the treasury of virtue.[1] I stated that the Brahmin must not be content with making money, for that would make him no longer a Brahmin, but rather someone who has forsaken his true calling.[1] I explained that the Brahmin must give to the people at large the accumulated culture of ages, as it was because he did not do so that the Mohammedan invasion was possible.[2] I urged the Brahmin to be the first to break open the cells that hide the wonderful treasures of our common ancestors and bring them out for the benefit of all.[2] I reminded the Brahmin that he must not be in a hurry to fight with the non-Brahmin castes, as they are suffering from their own faults and neglect of spirituality.[2] I emphasized that the Brahmin must not be content with his own privileges, but must work for the salvation of the rest of mankind in India, for that is the true Brahminhood.[1]

question: What did you say about Japan when you visited it?

result.text: I wrote to Alasinga from Hong Kong that from Canton I returned back to Hong Kong, and from thence to Japan.[1] I described Nagasaki as the first port we touched, where we landed for a few hours and drove through the town.[1] I remarked on the contrast between Japan and other places, noting that the Japanese are one of the cleanliest peoples on earth.[1] I observed that everything in Japan is neat and tidy, with broad, straight, and regularly paved streets.[1] I noted that the little houses in Japan are cage-like, and their pine-covered evergreen little hills form the background of almost every town and village.[1] I described the Japanese as short-statured, fair-skinned, and quaintly-dressed, with movements, attitudes, and gestures that are picturesque.[1] I stated that Japan is the land of the picturesque, with almost every house having a garden at the back, very nicely laid out according to Japanese fashion.[1] I wrote to Mr. Okakura Kakuzo that Japan to me is a dream — so beautiful that it haunts one all his life.[2] I told Miss Josephine Macleod that I am so glad she is enjoying Japan — especially Japanese art.[3] I wrote to Miss Mary Hale that I have seen Japan before, and that the rivers of East Bengal are oceans of rolling fresh water.[4]

question: What did you say about American women?

result.text: I have a good impression of this country especially of the American women.[1] I have especially remarked on the absence of poverty in America.[1] He praises the American women most enthusiastically.[2] I have heard many stories about the American home: of liberty running into licence, of unwomanly women smashing under their feet all the peace and happiness of home-life in their mad liberty-dance, and much nonsense of that type.[3] A hundred lives would not be sufficient to pay my deep debt of gratitude to you![3] Those emaciated Western women, looking like old dried-up fruit, whom you see in India, are English, and the English are an ugly race amongst the Europeans.[4] In America, the best blood strains of Europe have been blended, and therefore, the American women are very beautiful.[4] The average American woman is far more cultivated than the average American man.[5] In that country the women are more learned than men.[6] They are all well versed in science and philosophy, and that is why they would appreciate and honour me so much.[6]

question: What did you say about the Jains?

result.text: I spoke about the Jains in my lecture on the religions of India, highlighting their remarkable kindness to dumb animals and their moral law of not injuring others.[1] I emphasized that the Jains were the first great ascetics and that their principle of non-injury and doing good was the foundation of all ethics.[2] I noted that the Jains were a conservative force in India, even today, and that they challenged the validity of the Vedas, claiming their own books were the original Vedas.[3] I mentioned that the Jains wrote their books in Pali, and that Sanskrit had ceased to be a spoken language, much like Latin is to modern Italian.[3] I pointed out that the Jains were among the sects that believed in the soul but not in the moral government of the country, and that they had millions of followers in India.[4] I observed that the Jains were one of the few religious groups that still kept their traditions alive because of their books, alongside the Parsees.[5] I noted that the Jains were a sect that believed in the soul but were agnostic in relation to God, and that they had a unique practice of tying handkerchiefs over their faces.[4]

question: What did you write about the Paris Congress of the History of Religions?

result.text: I wrote about the Paris Congress of the History of Religions in a letter to Swami Turiyananda, where I mentioned that the session was not a big affair and that some twenty scholars discussed topics like the origin of the Shâlagrâma and Jehovah.[1] I also wrote that the Congress was attended only by scholars devoted to the study of the origin and history of different religions, unlike the Chicago Parliament of Religions, which had representatives from many religious sects.[2] I noted that the Paris Congress was similar to the Congress of Orientalists, with European scholars versed in Sanskrit, Pali, Arabic, and other Oriental languages, but with the addition of the antiquarianism of Christianity.[3] I was invited by the Paris Congress to contradict a certain conviction and promised to read a paper on the subject, though I could not keep my promise due to ill health and was only able to attend the Congress.[4] I wrote a poem in which I stated that I am an ignoramus and do not pretend to any scholarship, but I strongly protested against certain ideas at the Paris Congress and urged Indian and European savants to draw their own conclusions from their scriptures.[5]

question: What did you say about the Vedanta being practical?

result.text: I argued that the Vedanta philosophy must be intensely practical, as it must be carried out in every part of our lives.[1] I explained that the Vedanta teaches oneness — one life throughout, and the fictitious differentiation between religion and the life of the world must vanish.[1] I stated that the Vedanta, though it is intensely practical, is always so in the sense of the ideal, not an impossible one.[2] I emphasized that the Vedanta teaches men to have faith in themselves first, and that not believing in the glory of our own soul is what the Vedanta calls atheism.[2] I noted that the Vedanta says that each one must have his own path, but the path is not the goal, and that the worship of a God in heaven is only a step towards the Truth.[3] I pointed out that the Vedanta teaches no such thing as degrading the ideal to the actual, and that the actual should be reconciled to the ideal.[4] I mentioned that the Vedanta is the simplest form in which you can put truth, and that teaching dualism was a tremendous mistake made in India.[5] I said that the practical side of all religions is found in the lives of the saints, and that practice, work, will bring us up to the vision of the Divine.[6]

question: What did you say about Kali and Mother worship?

result.text: I wrote to Miss Mary Hale from Los Angeles on June 17, 1900, that Kâli worship is not a necessary step in any religion.[1] I told Sharat Chandra Chakravarty that the figure of Mother Kali represents the union of the blissful and the terrible aspects, though none of the pictures can adequately express these.[2] I blessed Swami Brahmananda on the night sacred to the Divine Mother, urging him to let the Mother dance in his heart and bring infinite strength to his arms.[3] I performed a Homa before the Mother Kali at Kalighat, and the temple authorities welcomed me warmly despite knowing I had returned from the West.[4] I told Sharat Chandra Chakravarty that Kali is Brahman in manifestation, and I referenced Shri Ramakrishna's illustration of the 'snake moving and the snake at rest' to explain this.[5] I wrote to Swami Brahmananda that I am the servant of the Mother, and you are all servants of the Mother — what destruction, what fear is there for us?[6] I told Sharat Chandra Chakravarty that I have tried to put down some ideas of the terrible aspects of Mother Kali in my English poem, Kali the Mother.[2]

question: What did you say about the hymn 'As the different streams having their sources in different places'?

result.text: I quoted to you, brethren, a few lines from a hymn which I remember to have repeated from my earliest boyhood, which is every day repeated by millions and millions of men in India.[1] I will quote to you, brethren, a few lines from a hymn which I remember to have repeated from my earliest boyhood, which is every day repeated by millions of human beings: 'As the different streams having their sources in different places all mingle their water in the sea, so, O Lord, the different paths which men take through different tendencies, various though they appear, crooked or straight, all lead to Thee.'[1] I will quote to you, brethren, a few lines from a hymn which every Hindoo child repeats every day.[2] As the different streams having their sources in different places all mingle their water in the sea, so, O Lord, the different paths which men take through different tendencies, various though they appear, crooked or straight, all lead to Thee.[1] As the different streams having their sources in different places all mingle their water in the sea, so, O Lord, the different paths which men take through different tendencies, various though they appear, crooked or straight, all lead to Thee.[2] As the different streams, having their sources in different places, all mingle their water in the sea; O Lord, so the different paths which men take through different tendencies, various though they appear, crooked or straight, all lead to Thee.[2] As the different rivers, taking their start from different mountains, running crooked or straight, all come and mingle their waters in the ocean, so the different sects, with their different points of view, at last all come unto Thee.[3] As so many rivers, having their source in different mountains, roll down, crooked or straight, and at last come into the ocean — so, all these various creeds and religions, taking their start from different standpoints and running through crooked or straight courses, at last come unto THEE.[4]

question: What did you say about the Gita and Krishna's historicity?

result.text: I told the audience at Chicago that Krishna was a married man, and there are thousands of books about him, but they do not interest me much.[1] I explained that the Hindus are great in telling stories, and if the Christian missionaries tell one story from their Bible, the Hindus will produce twenty stories.[1] I stated that since I was a child I have heard about Krishna's life, and I take it for granted there must have been a man called Krishna, and his Gita shows he has left a wonderful book.[1] I argued that you can understand the character of a man by analysing the fables about him, and the fables have the nature of decorations, polished and manipulated to fit into the character.[1] I noted that the central idea of Krishna is non-attachment, and he does not need anything, does not want anything, and works for work's sake.[1] I wrote to Mr. __ from Almora that the Gita has become the Bible of Hinduism, but the personality of Krishna has become so covered with haze that it is impossible today to draw any life-giving inspiration from that life.[2] I mentioned that the Gita forms a part of the Mahâbhârata, and to understand it properly, several things are very important to know, including whether there was any historical personality of the name of Krishna.[3] I stated that it is human nature to build round the real character of a great man all sorts of imaginary superhuman attributes, and it seems quite probable that Krishna was a king.[4] I noted that the Gita harmonizes all these conflicting doctrines, and as to Krishna, whether or not he ever lived, I do not know.[5]

question: How did you define religion in your lectures?

result.text: I defined religion as realisation, not mere talk or parroting the words of ancestors.[1] I said that religion is the most wonderful factor in the social organism, and that knowledge of God and the soul is the highest gain.[2] I explained that religion is not about one creed, but about the realisation of the soul and the understanding of man's own nature.[2] I argued that religion is not a political something, but a spiritual realisation that transcends all sects.[1] I stated that the Vedantic religion takes in all types of religion, allowing each person to choose according to their nature.[2] I said that the only true teacher is one who can transfer his soul to the student's soul and understand through their eyes and ears.[1] I explained that religion is not about one religion for the whole world, but about the variety of religious thought being its life.[2]

question: What did you say about the problem of evil?

result.text: As I spoke at the lecture on Worshipper and Worshipped, I addressed the question of why there is evil, stating that the only way to solve this problem is by acknowledging that God is the cause of both good and evil.[1] I explained that the difficulty in the theory of the Personal God arises when one insists that God is only good, which leads to the trap of one's own argument.[1] In my lecture on Discipleship, I emphasized that good and evil always exist in the world, and that denying or ignoring evil is a weakness stemming from fear.[2] I argued that God has placed evil in the world, but we do not need to whitewash Him or explain why evil exists.[2] In a letter to Miss Mary Hale, I expressed that I enjoy both good and evil, seeing them as part of a game or play, and that all is good.[3] I stated that understanding only gives us good or evil, but I am beyond such distinctions, being peace that passeth understanding.[3] In my lecture on The Soul and God, I noted that people often blame others for their mistakes, such as attributing actions to the devil rather than taking responsibility.[4] I acknowledged that some may think evil actions are good, but this does not remove their evil tendencies.[5]

question: What did you say about hypnotism and psychic powers?

result.text: I told Sharat Chandra Chakravarty that it is terrible hypnotism to think the soul has any sex, and that it is self-hypnotism to believe one is men or women.[1] I explained to Shri Priya Nath Sinha that Western disciples have developed spiritual and psychic powers very quickly through the Sâdhanâs practiced for only four months.[2] I remarked to Sharat Chandra Chakravarty that it is a shame to have to strengthen one's belief in the hereafter by seeing ghosts and spirits, even with so much knowledge of the universe.[3] I told the audience at the Graduate Philosophical Society that what the West calls hypnotism is only a part of the real thing, and that the Hindus call it self-hypnotisation.[4] I described to the audience at the Graduate Philosophical Society that the Advaitist alone does not care to be hypnotised, and that his system understands hypnotism comes with every form of dualism.[4] I told the audience at the Graduate Philosophical Society that the Advaitist says to throw away even the Vedas, the Personal God, the universe, and one's own body and mind, in order to get rid of hypnotism perfectly.[4] I told the audience at the Graduate Philosophical Society that the Advaitist says, 'I have neither vice nor virtue, nor misery nor happiness; I care neither for the Vedas nor sacrifices nor ceremonies; I am neither food nor eating nor eater, for I am Existence Absolute, Knowledge Absolute, Bliss Absolute; I am He, I am He.'[4]

question: What did you tell the Alambazar Math members about rules of the monastery?

result.text: I wrote to the members of the Alambazar Math from High View on April 27, 1896, that if they followed my ideas and rules, I would supply all necessary funds for their work.[1] I emphasized that they should show my letter to Gour-Mâ, Yogin-Mâ, and others, and through them establish a Women's Math, with Gour-Ma as the President for one year.[1] I warned them that none of them should be allowed to visit the Women's Math, as they would manage their own affairs independently.[1] In the same letter, I expressed that my purpose was not for personal authority, but for their good and for fulfilling the purpose for which the Lord came.[2] I cautioned them against jealousy and egotism, stating that it would be a pity if such feelings gained ground among them.[2] I mentioned that it is natural for idle minds to indulge in gossip and faction-mongering, and that it is necessary at the immature stage to be guided by rules.[2] I used the analogy of the sapling being hedged round, as the Master used to say, to explain the need for guidance at the early stage.[2]

question: What did you say about Mahavira and Indian history?

result.text: I told Sarat Chandra Chakravarty that we have to introduce the worship of the great saints, such as Mahâvira, as the ideas to be followed in India.[1] I emphasized that Mahâvira was a great-souled one who had realized the eternal truths and should be presented before the people as an ideal to be followed.[1] I urged that the worship of Mahâvira should be spread far and wide, highlighting his role as a perfect master of his senses and wonderfully sagacious.[1] I spoke of Mahâvira as an ideal of personal service, through which all other ideals will gradually manifest in life.[2] I mentioned that Mahâvira had no care for life or death and was a supreme example of devotion to the service of Rama.[2] I called upon people to build their lives on the great ideal of Mahâvira, who was a perfect example of selflessness and courage.[2]

question: What did you write about the East and the West in your essay?

result.text: I wrote about the East and the West in my essay, highlighting the irony of the teachings of Jesus Christ and Krishna, which were not taken seriously by the Europeans.[1] I noted that the Europeans, with their Râjasika nature, are gathering the comforts and luxuries of the world and enjoying them to their hearts' content, while we are pondering on death day and night.[1] I emphasized that the Europeans never took the words of Jesus Christ seriously, and that they are always of active habits, being possessed of a tremendous Râjasika nature.[1] I compared the two nations, stating that they are both good, and that neither can be praised nor blamed, as both the scales are equal.[2] I mentioned that there are gradations and varieties of good, and that both the East and the West have their own strengths and weaknesses.[2] I wrote that the Europeans have not taken the teachings of Jesus Christ seriously, and that they are always of active habits, being possessed of a tremendous Râjasika nature.[1]

question: What did you say about the Arya Samaj and Dayananda?

result.text: I wrote to Miss Mary Hale from Ridgely Manor on 1899-10-30 that the Arya Samaj and other sects were useless mixtures, only voices of apology to our English masters to allow us to live.[1] I noted in my writings that the Arya Samaj, founded by a Sannyasin, was a movement that left us wondering about the creation of a body of teachers for the new movement in the Punjab.[2] I mentioned in my lectures that the Arya Samaj was one of the sects that, along with the Brahmo Samaj and others, had been part of the waves of religious change in India, which had been revolutionizing society in the name of religion.[3] I wrote to Mr.__ from Almora on 1897-06-01 that Swami Dayananda thought he could find a consistent theory of the whole based on a new interpretation of the Samhitas, but the difficulties remained the same, only they fell back on the Brahmanas.[4]

question: What did you say about Tantra and the Tantras?

result.text: I have no faith in the theories advanced by Western savants with regard to the Vedas.[1] I denounced only the present corrupted form of Vâmâchâra of the Tantras.[2] The Tantras, as we have said, represent the Vedic rituals in a modified form.[3] The real meaning of the word Tantra is Shâstra, as for example, Kâpila Tantra.[1] I denounced only these corrupt and horrible practices — which I do even now.[2] The Tantras are not so bad as people are inclined to think.[1] The Tantras were the creation of the Buddhists themselves.[4] The Tantras contain many beautiful and illuminating teachings and words of wisdom on Yoga, Bhakti, Jnâna, and Karma.[1] The Tantras are influenced by the ideas of the corrupted Vamachara.[2]

question: What did you say about spiritualism and talking to the dead?

result.text: I wrote to the editor of Light that the truth of correspondence between the living and the dead is in every religion, and nowhere more than in the Vedantic sects of India.[1] I expressed my admiration for the Spiritualist community for the positive good they have done, such as preaching universal sympathy and helping the human race out of doctrines that inculcate fear and not love.[1] I mentioned that I have attended several spiritualistic meetings, and in one, a woman claimed that my mother and grandfather came to her and talked to her.[2] I expressed my sorrow that people might think their dead relatives are still wearing their filthy bodies, and that spiritualists play on their superstitions.[2] I told Sharat Chandra Chakravarty that it is a shame for even heroes to strengthen their belief in the hereafter by seeing ghosts and spirits.[3] I recounted an experience at a seance where a medium claimed to see a ghost, but I pointed out that no ghost was needed to tell them that a Hindu gentleman was on the bench.[4]

question: What did you say about the poverty of your own family?

result.text: I wrote to Miss Mary Hale from Pasadena on February 20, 1900, that I had been in the glare, burning and panting all the time, and that my life was made up of continuous blows like that, and hundred times worse, because of poverty, treachery, and my own foolishness.[1] In my lecture on 'My Life and Mission,' I spoke of a terrible time when my father died and we were left poor, almost starving all the time.[2] I told the audience at the Belur Math that the real evil is idleness, which is the principal cause of our poverty.[3] I wrote to Ramakrishnananda from Cape Comorin that I had no sleep due to the poverty and ignorance of the people, and that we were so many Sannyasins wandering about, teaching the people metaphysics — it was all madness.[4] In my poem 'To a Friend,' I described myself as friendless, clad in rags, with no possession, feeding from door to door on what chance would bring.[5]

question: What did you say about the Chicago Fair and your early days in America?

result.text: I wrote to Alasinga from Breezy Meadows on August 20, 1893, describing my journey from Japan to Vancouver, then through Canada to Chicago, where I spent twelve days and visited the Fair almost every day.[1] I told the interviewer at India's Mission that I was the Hindu representative at the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago in 1893, sent by the Raja of Mysore and other friends, and that I had many invitations to other American cities besides Chicago.[2] In my interview with India and England, I mentioned that the World's Parliament of Religions was held in Chicago at the time of the World's Fair instead of in London, and that I stayed in America for three years with the exception of visits to England.[3] I described a funny incident in Chicago where the Raja of Kapurthala was being lionised, and an eccentric Mahratta Brahmin sold nail-made pictures in the Fair, leading to a situation where newspaper editors used my name to give my countryman a brushing.[4] In my lecture in Calcutta, I mentioned that at the great Parliament of Religions in Chicago in 1893, I presented the principles of the Aryan religion, which was a revelation to many in the audience.[5] I told the interviewer at India's Mission that I got thoroughly used to the interviewer in America, and that the American mind is peculiarly susceptible to new ideas, which is examined on its own merits.[2] In my interview with The Missionary Work of the First Hindu Sannyasin, I was asked about my early life, but I did not provide details in that context.[6]

question: What did you say about your health and illness in your last years?

result.text: I wrote to Sister Christine from Ridgely Manor on October 30, 1899, asking if she had received my last letter and expressing my concern for her health.[1] I wrote to Sister Christine from The Math on October 25, 1898, asking how she was and expressing my anxiety about her health.[2] I wrote to Maharaja Ajit Singh from Srinagar on August 10, 1898, inquiring about his health and how things were going with him.[3] I wrote to Swami Ramakrishnananda from Ambala on August 19, 1897, mentioning that my health had been very bad recently but that I was slowly recovering.[4] I wrote to Your Highness from Almora on June 9, 1898, expressing my regret at learning that you were not in perfect health and assuring you that you would be soon.[5] I wrote to Sister Christine from The Math on January 26, 1899, explaining that I had been in the vale of death and that my old diabetes had been replaced by a worrying disease causing suffocation.[6] I told Sharat Chandra Chakravarty that my body was getting unfit for work and that I was born on the soil of Bengal, where some disease or other was always overtaking me.[7] I wrote to Sister Christine from Suez on July 14, 1899, describing my poor health in India and the terrible fits of asthma I had experienced.[8] I told Sharat Chandra Chakravarty that I had just returned from East Bengal and Assam and was ill, with swollen feet, but still wore my usual smiling face and affectionate look.[9]

question: What did you say about music and art in India?

result.text: I wrote in my lecture on art in India that music was developed to the full seven notes, even to half and quarter notes, ages ago.[1] I noted that India led in music, also in drama and sculpture, and that whatever is done now is merely an attempt at imitation.[1] I explained that in India, music and drama are themselves held to be religion, and that any song, if one's whole soul is in it, leads to salvation.[2] I mentioned that the Mohammedans took up the different Râgas and Râginis after coming into India, but they put such a stamp of their own colouring on the art of Tappa songs that all the science in music was destroyed.[3] I stated that in India, it is better to be absorbed in music or in literature than in comfort or pleasure, and we never say otherwise.[4] I remarked that the Asian never uses a thing unless there be art in it, and that art is, with us, a part of religion.[5] I observed that in India, the very soul of the Asian is interwoven with art, and that what we still have is wonderful despite having lost almost everything.[5]

question: What is Jnana-Yoga?

result.text:
I spoke to this in my lecture The First Step Towards Jnana, in 1900.
“The word Jnâna means knowledge. It is derived from the root Jnâ — to know — the same word from which your English word to know is derived. Jnana-Yoga is Yoga by means of knowledge. What is the object of the Jnana-Yoga? Freedom. Freedom from what? Freedom from our imperfections, freedom from the misery of life. Why are we miserable? We are miserable because we are bound. What is the bondage? The bondage is of nature. Who is it that binds us? We, ourselves.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 6, Lectures and Discourses, Introduction to Jnana-Yoga]; [Vol 8, Lectures and Discourses, Jnana Yoga].

question: What is the secret of work?

result.text:
In Karma-Yoga I set it down thus.
“What is Karma-Yoga? The knowledge of the secret of work. We see that the whole universe is working. For what? For salvation, for liberty; from the atom to the highest being, working for the one end, liberty for the mind, for the body, for the spirit. All things are always trying to get freedom, flying away from bondage. The sun, the moon, the earth, the planets, all are trying to fly away from bondage. The centrifugal and the centripetal forces of nature are indeed typical of our universe. Instead of being knocked about in this universe, and after long delay and thrashing, getting to know things as they are, we learn from Karma-Yoga the secret of work, the method of work, the organising power of work. A vast mass of energy may be spent in vain if we do not know how to utilise it.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Karma-Yoga, Ch. 3: The Secret of Work]; [Vol 1, Karma-Yoga, Ch. 1: Karma in Its Effect on Character].

question: What is duty?

result.text:
In Karma-Yoga I set it down thus.
“It is necessary in the study of Karma-Yoga to know what duty is. If I have to do something I must first know that it is my duty, and then I can do it. The idea of duty again is different in different nations. The Mohammedan says what is written in his book, the Koran, is his duty; the Hindu says what is in the Vedas is his duty; and the Christian says what is in the Bible is his duty. We find that there are varied ideas of duty, differing according to different states in life, different historical periods and different nations. The term "duty", like every other universal abstract term, is impossible clearly to define; we can only get an idea of it by knowing its practical operations and results. When certain things occur before us, we have all a natural or trained impulse to act in a certain manner towards them; when this impulse comes, the mind begins to think about the situation. Sometimes it thinks that it is good to act in a particular manner under the given conditions; at other times it thinks that it is wrong to act in the same manner even in the very same circumstances. The ordinary idea of duty everywhere is that every good man follows the dictates of his conscience. But what is it that makes an act a duty?” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Karma-Yoga, Ch. 7: Freedom]; [Vol 1, Karma-Yoga, Ch. 2: Each Is Great in His Own Place].

question: What is Maya?

result.text:
This is how I treated it in Jnana-Yoga.
“We have seen how the idea of Mâyâ, which forms, as it were, one of the basic doctrines of the Advaita Vedanta, is, in its germs, found even in the Samhitâs, and that in reality all the ideas which are developed in the Upanishads are to be found already in the Samhitas in some form or other. Most of you are by this time familiar with the idea of Maya, and know that it is sometimes erroneously explained as illusion, so that when the universe is said to be Maya, that also has to be explained as being illusion. The translation of the word is neither happy nor correct. Maya is not a theory; it is simply a statement of facts about the universe as it exists, and to understand Maya we must go back to the Samhitas and begin with the conception in the germ.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 2, Jnana-Yoga, Ch. 3: Maya and Illusion].

question: What is Prana?

result.text:
My hearers recorded me saying this in Lessons on Raja-Yoga.
“The name of the energy in the universe is Prâna, which is the force residing in these elements. Mind is the great instrument for using the Prana. Mind is material. Behind the mind is Âtman which takes hold of the Prana. Prana is the driving power of the world, and can be seen in every manifestation of life. The body is mortal and the mind is mortal; both, being compounds, must die. Behind all is the Atman which never dies. The Atman is pure intelligence controlling and directing Prana. But the intelligence we see around us is always imperfect. When intelligence is perfect, we get the Incarnation — the Christ. Intelligence is always trying to manifest itself, and in order to do this it is creating minds and bodies of different degrees of development. In reality, and at the back of all things, every being is equal.” [1]

question: What is the goal of Raja-Yoga?

result.text:
In Raja-Yoga I set it down thus.
“According to Yoga philosophy, it is through ignorance that the soul has been joined with nature. The aim is to get rid of nature's control over us. That is the goal of all religions. Each soul is potentially divine. The goal is to manifest this Divinity within, by controlling nature, external and internal. Do this either by work, or worship, or psychic control, or philosophy — by one or more or all of these — and be free. This is the whole of religion. Doctrines, or dogmas, or rituals, or books, or temples, or forms, are but secondary details. The Yogi tries to reach this goal through psychic control. Until we can free ourselves from nature, we are slaves; as she dictates so we must go. The Yogi claims that he who controls mind controls matter also. The internal nature is much higher than the external and much more difficult to grapple with, much more difficult to control. Therefore he who has conquered the internal nature controls the whole universe; it becomes his servant. Raja-Yoga propounds the methods of gaining this control. Forces higher than we know in physical nature will have to be subdued. This body is just the external crust of the mind.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Raja-Yoga, Preface]; [Vol 1, Raja-Yoga, Ch. 7: Dhyana and Samadhi].

question: What is Pratyahara?

result.text:
In Raja-Yoga I set it down thus.
“The organs are separate states of the mind-stuff. I see a book; the form is not in the book, it is in the mind. Something is outside which calls that form up. The real form is in the Chitta. The organs identify themselves with, and take the forms of, whatever comes to them. If you can restrain the mind-stuff from taking these forms, the mind will remain calm. This is called Pratyahara.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Raja-Yoga, Ch. 6: Pratyahara and Dharana]; [Vol 1, Raja-Yoga, Ch. 8: Raja-Yoga in Brief].

question: What is Samadhi?

result.text:
This is how I treated it in Raja-Yoga.
“Samadhi is the property of every human being — nay, every animal. From the lowest animal to the highest angel, some time or other, each one will have to come to that state, and then, and then alone, will real religion begin for him. Until then we only struggle towards that stage. There is no difference now between us and those who have no religion, because we have no experience. What is concentration good for, save to bring us to this experience? Each one of the steps to attain Samadhi has been reasoned out, properly adjusted, scientifically organised, and, when faithfully practiced, will surely lead us to the desired end. Then will all sorrows cease, all miseries vanish; the seeds for actions will be burnt, and the soul will be free for ever.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Raja-Yoga, Patanjali's Yoga Aphorisms].

question: What is the Atman?

result.text:
I wrote of this in Jnana-Yoga, in the chapter Ch. 2: The Real Nature of Man.
“We will take the present theme. What is this force which is now working through us? We know how in old times, in all the ancient scriptures, this power, this manifestation of power, was thought to be a bright substance having the form of this body, and which remained even after this body fell. Later on, however, we find a higher idea coming — that this bright body did not represent the force. Whatsoever has form must be the result of combinations of particles and requires something else behind it to move it. If this body requires something which is not the body to manipulate it, the bright body, by the same necessity, will also require something other than itself to manipulate it. So, that something was called the soul, the Atman in Sanskrit. It was the Atman which through the bright body, as it were, worked on the gross body outside. The bright body is considered as the receptacle of the mind, and the Atman is beyond that It is not the mind even; it works the mind, and through the mind the body. You have an Atman, I have another each one of us has a separate Atman and a separate fine body, and through that we work on the gross external body. Questions were then asked about this Atman about its nature.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 2, Jnana-Yoga, Ch. 14: The Atman: Its Bondage and Freedom].

question: What is the real nature of man?

result.text:
In Jnana-Yoga I set it down thus.
“We are not individuals yet. We are struggling towards individuality, and that is the Infinite, that is the real nature of man. He alone lives whose life is in the whole universe, and the more we concentrate our lives on limited things, the faster we go towards death. Those moments alone we live when our lives are in the universe, in others; and living this little life is death, simply death, and that is why the fear of death comes. The fear of death can only be conquered when man realises that so long as there is one life in this universe, he is living. When he can say, "I am in everything, in everybody, I am in all lives, I am the universe," then alone comes the state of fearlessness. To talk of immortality in constantly changing things is absurd. Says an old Sanskrit philosopher: It is only the Spirit that is the individual, because it is infinite. No infinity can be divided; infinity cannot be broken into pieces. It is the same one, undivided unit for ever, and this is the individual man, the Real Man. The apparent man is merely a struggle to express, to manifest this individuality which is beyond; and evolution is not in the Spirit. These changes which are going on — the wicked becoming good, the animal becoming man, take them in whatever way you like — are not in the Spirit. They are evolution of nature and manifestation of Spirit.” [1]

question: What is the ideal of a universal religion?

result.text:
I spoke to this in my lecture The Ideal of a Universal Religion.
“What then do I mean by the ideal of a universal religion? I do not mean any one universal philosophy, or any one universal mythology, or any one universal ritual held alike by all; for I know that this world must go on working, wheel within wheel, this intricate mass of machinery, most complex, most wonderful. What can we do then? We can make it run smoothly, we can lessen the friction, we can grease the wheels, as it were. How? By recognising the natural necessity of variation. Just as we have recognised unity by our very nature, so we must also recognise variation. We must learn that truth may be expressed in a hundred thousand ways, and that each of these ways is true as far as it goes. We must learn that the same thing can be viewed from a hundred different standpoints, and vet be the same thing. Take for instance the sun. Suppose a man standing on the earth looks at the sun when it rises in the morning; he sees a big ball. Suppose he starts on a journey towards the sun and takes a camera with him, taking photographs at every stage of his journey, until he reaches the sun.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 2, Practical Vedanta and Other Lectures, The Way to the Realisation of a Universal Religion].

question: What is the difference between religion and the religions?

result.text: Religion is the acceptance of all existing creeds, seeing in them the same striving towards the same destination. Creed is something antagonistic and combative. There are different creeds, because there are different people, and the creed is adapted to the commonwealth where it furnishes what people want. As the world is made up of infinite variety of persons of different natures, intellectually, spiritually, and materially, so these people take to themselves that form of belief in the existence of a great and good moral law, which is best fitted for them. Religion recognises and is glad of the existence of all these forms because of the beautiful underlying principle. The same goal is reached by different routes and my way would not be suited perhaps to the temperament of my Western neighbour, the same that his route would not commend itself to my disposition and philosophical way of thinking.

question: What is renunciation?

result.text:
I put it this way in my address Christ, the Messenger.
“This is the great lesson of the Messenger, and another which is the basis of all religions, is renunciation. How can you make the spirit pure? By renunciation. A rich young man asked Jesus, "Good Master, what shall I do that I may inherit eternal life?" And Jesus said unto him, "One thing thou lackest; go thy way, sell whatsoever thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasures in heaven: and come, take up thy cross, and follow Me." And he was sad at that saying and went away grieved; for he had great possessions. We are all more or less like that. The voice is ringing in our ears day and night. In the midst of our pleasures and joys, in the midst of worldly things, we think that we have forgotten everything else. Then comes a moment's pause and the voice rings in our ears "Give up all that thou hast and follow Me." "Whosoever will save his life shall lose it; and whosoever shall lose his life for My sake shall find it." For whoever gives up this life for His sake, finds the life immortal. In the midst of all our weakness there is a moment of pause and the voice rings: "Give up all that thou hast; give it to the poor and follow me." This is the one ideal he preaches, and this has been the ideal preached by all the great Prophets of the world: renunciation.” [1]

A rich young man asked Jesus, "Good Master, what shall I do that I may inherit eternal life?" And Jesus said unto him, "One thing thou lackest; go thy way, sell whatsoever thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasures in heaven: and come, take up thy cross, and follow Me." And he was sad at that saying and went away grieved; for he had great possessions. We are all more or less like that. The voice is ringing in our ears day and night. In the midst of our pleasures and joys, in the midst of worldly things, we think that we have forgotten everything else. Then comes a moment's pause and the voice rings in our ears "Give up all that thou hast and follow Me." "Whosoever will save his life shall lose it; and whosoever shall lose his life for My sake shall find it." For whoever gives up this life for His sake, finds the life immortal. In the midst of all our weakness there is a moment of pause and the voice rings: "Give up all that thou hast; give it to the poor and follow me." This is the one ideal he preaches, and this has been the ideal preached by all the great Prophets of the world: renunciation.

question: What is Para-Bhakti?

result.text:
I wrote of this in Para-Bhakti or Supreme Devotion, in the chapter Ch. 6: The Higher Knowledge and the Higher Love Are One to the True Lover.
“The higher knowledge is thus clearly shown to be the knowledge of the Brahman; and the Devi-Bhâgavata gives us the following definition of the higher love (Para-Bhakti): "As oil poured from one vessel to another falls in an unbroken line, so, when the mind in an unbroken stream thinks of the Lord, we have what is called Para-Bhakti or supreme love." This kind of undisturbed and ever-steady direction of the mind and the heart to the Lord with an inseparable attachment is indeed the highest manifestation of man's love to God. All other forms of Bhakti are only preparatory to the attainment of this highest form thereof, viz the Para-Bhakti which is also known as the love that comes after attachment (Râgânugâ). When this supreme love once comes into the heart of man, his mind will continuously think of God and remember nothing else. He will give no room in himself to thoughts other than those of God, and his soul will be unconquerably pure and will alone break all the bonds of mind and matter and become serenely free.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 3, Para-Bhakti or Supreme Devotion, Ch. 1: The Preparatory Renunciation]; [Vol 3, Para-Bhakti or Supreme Devotion, Ch. 2: The Bhakta's Renunciation Results from Love].

question: What is the Ishta?

result.text:
I spoke to this in my lecture The Ishta, in 1900.
“The theory of Ishta, which I briefly referred to before, is a subject requiring careful attention because with a proper understanding of this, all the various religions of the world can be understood. The word Ishta is derived from the root Ish, to desire, choose. The ideal of all religions, all sects, is the same — the attaining of liberty and cessation of misery. Wherever you find religion, you find this ideal working in one form or other. Of course in lower stages of religion it is not so well expressed; but still, well or ill-expressed, it is the one goal to which every religion approaches. All of us want to get rid of misery; we are struggling to attain to liberty — physical, mental, spiritual. This is the whole idea upon which the world is working. Through the goal is one and the same, there may be many ways to reach it, and these ways are determined by the peculiarities of our nature. One man's nature is emotional, another's intellectual, another's active, and so forth. Again, in the same nature there may be many subdivisions. Take for instance love, with which we are specially concerned in this subject of Bhakti. One man's nature has a stronger love for children; another has it for wife, another for mother, another for father, another for friends.” [1]

question: What is the need of a Guru?

result.text:
In Bhakti-Yoga I set it down thus.
“Every soul is destined to be perfect, and every being, in the end, will attain the state of perfection. Whatever we are now is the result of our acts and thoughts in the past; and whatever we shall be in the future will be the result of what we think end do now. But this, the shaping of our own destinies, does not preclude our receiving help from outside; nay, in the vast majority of cases such help is absolutely necessary. When it comes, the higher powers and possibilities of the soul are quickened, spiritual life is awakened, growth is animated, and man becomes holy and perfect in the end.” [1]

question: What is the cause of evil in the world?

result.text:
I wrote of this in Jnana-Yoga, in the chapter Ch. 13: The Atman.
“With all dualistic theories the first difficulty is, how is it possible that under the rule of a just and merciful God, the repository of an infinite number of good qualities, there can be so many evils in this world? This question arose in all dualistic religions, but the Hindus never invented a Satan as an answer to it. The Hindus with one accord laid the blame on man, and it was easy for them to do so. Why? Because, as I have just now told you, they did not believe that souls were created out of nothing We see in this life that we can shape and form our future every one of us, every day, is trying to shape the morrow; today we fix the fate of the morrow; tomorrow we shall fix the fate of the day after, and so on. It is quite logical that this reasoning can be pushed backward too. If by our own deeds we shape our destiny in the future why not apply the same rule to the past? If, in an infinite chain, a certain number of links are alternately repeated then, if one of these groups of links be explained, we can explain the whole chain. So, in this infinite length of time, if we can cut off one portion and explain that portion and understand it, then, if it be true that nature is uniform, the same explanation must apply to the whole chain of time.” [1]

question: What is freedom?

result.text:
My hearers recorded me saying this in Freedom of the Self.
“As we cannot know except through effects that we have eyes, so we cannot see the Self except by Its effects. It cannot be brought down to the low plane of sense-perception. It is the condition of everything in the universe, though Itself unconditioned. When we know that we are the Self, then we are free. The Self can never change. It cannot be acted on by a cause, because It is Itself the cause. It is self-caused. If we can find in ourself something that is not acted on by any cause, then we have known the Self.” [1]
